name: Aranatha
summary: Jains revere Aranatha as the 18th Tirthankara of this age, born in Hastinapur and counted as a world-emperor. His name means a spoke of a wheel, from his mother's dream.
about: According to Jain tradition, Aranatha was born in Hastinapur to King Sudarshana and his queen, of the Ikshvaku line. Svetambara texts say his name Ara, a wheel's spoke, comes from a dream his mother had of a jewelled wheel. Jain texts also count him as the seventh chakravartin, ruler of the whole earth. They say a change of seasons made him think about how nothing lasts, so he gave up his empire, wandered as an ascetic for three years, reached omniscience and taught for about twenty-one thousand years. Jains believe he attained liberation on Mount Shikharji. His image stands in the four-faced Chaturmukha Basadi of Karkala.
kidSummary: Aranatha is remembered by Jains as the 18th Tirthankara. His name means a spoke of a wheel, because of his mother's dream of a shining wheel. The stories say he ruled the whole earth and then gave it up to learn how to stay calm and kind.

story.title: A dream of a wheel
story.text: Jain texts say his mother dreamed of a wheel set with gems. The baby was named Ara, which means a spoke of a wheel.

story.title: Emperor of six lands
story.text: He grew up in Hastinapur and became king. When a divine disc appeared in his armoury, he conquered the lands around, and thirty-two thousand kings stood with him.

story.title: Thinking about seasons
story.text: Jain accounts say he was watching the seasons change when he realised that nothing in life stays the same, not wealth, not power, not even glory.

story.title: Three years of wandering
story.text: He gave everything up and went into the forest as an ascetic. After about three years as an ordinary ascetic, he sat under a mango tree and, Jains believe, reached perfect knowledge.

story.title: A teacher for ages
story.text: He taught how to overcome attachment and dislike, which the texts call the real enemies. At the end, Jains believe, he reached liberation on Mount Shikharji.

facts.text: Ara means a spoke of a wheel. Jainworld says his mother saw a gem-studded wheel in her dreams, beyond the usual fourteen, and that gave the baby his name.
A 157 CE inscription on a Mathura stupa records an image of Aranatha, though two medieval writers attributed that stupa to Suparshvanatha instead.
At Karkala's Chaturmukha Basadi, built in 1586, life-size images of Aranatha, Mallinatha and Munisuvrata stand in a four-sided temple and are said to face the four cardinal directions.
Svetambara sources give his emblem as the nandyavarta, one of the eight auspicious symbols, while Digambara sources give a fish. A possible Mathura-era image shows paired fish on its base.
Hastinapur is tied to three Jinas who were world-emperors: Shanti, Kunthu and Ara. Its main Svetambara temple puts Shantinatha in the centre with Kunthu and Ara on either side.
Records from 1318 and 1333 CE tell of a pilgrimage and new images at Hastinapur. The poet Banarasidas describes his own 1618 pilgrimage there in an autobiography of 1641.
The Digambara hymn Svayambhustotra praises his form as free of ornaments, clothes and weapons, and reads that plainness as a sign that every inner fault has been conquered.
Stone sculptures carrying his Digambara fish emblem survive in the Khandagiri caves of Orissa and in Karnataka temples at Mudbidri and Karkala.

quiz.q: What does the name Ara mean?
quiz.why: Ara means a spoke of a wheel, from his mother's dream.

quiz.q: What did Aranatha reflect on before renouncing, in one Jain account?
quiz.why: Reflecting on the changing seasons made him feel that nothing lasts.

quiz.q: In one telling, what did Aranatha find when he went to carve his name on a mountain?
options: Names of earlier world-emperors already there
quiz.why: Finding earlier names humbled him, and he renounced his empire.

quiz.q: Which three Jinas are said to have been born at Hastinapur?
quiz.why: Hastinapur is the birthplace of Shantinatha, Kunthunatha and Aranatha.

quiz.q: Under which tree do Jains say he reached omniscience?
quiz.why: Jain texts say he reached omniscience under a mango tree.
